blocks.x: STAT 153 · Statistical Methods · Topic 5

Almost every question in medical statistics — how many patients arrive in an hour, how many test kits in a batch are defective, how many patients respond to a treatment — is really a question about a random variable. This topic gives you the formal machinery (PMF, CDF, expectation, variance) and the four named discrete distributions you will use again and again: Bernoulli, Binomial, Multinomial and Poisson.

By the end of this module, you will be able to…

items: 1Define a random variable and distinguish a discrete random variable (count data, e.g. number of patients) from a continuous random variable (measured data, e.g. height or weight).
2State and apply the probability mass function (PMF) of a discrete random variable, and derive the cumulative distribution function (CDF) F(x) = P(X ≤ x) from it.
3Compute the expected value (mean) and variance of a discrete random variable from first principles, using E(X) = Σx·p(x) and Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]².
4Recognise the conditions for a Bernoulli trial, a Binomial experiment, a Multinomial experiment and a Poisson process, and match a real (often clinical) scenario to the correct distribution.

5Apply the PMF, mean and variance formulas of the Bernoulli, Binomial, Multinomial and Poisson distributions to compute probabilities in worked, exam-style problems — including hospital quality-control and patient-arrival scenarios.
6Use the Poisson approximation to the Binomial distribution when n is large and p is small, and justify why it simplifies the computation.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Random variable A random variable X is a variable whose value is a numerical outcome of a random phenomenon or experiment. It assigns a real number to every outcome in the sample space. Random variables are classified as discrete or continuous.

Discrete random variable A random variable X is discrete if it can take on only a finite or countably infinite number of distinct values (usually whole numbers obtained by counting). Discrete random variables typically represent count data — e.g. the number of patients in a hospital, the number of defective test kits in a batch, or the number of successes in n trials.

Continuous random variable A random variable X is continuous if it can assume infinitely many values within an interval of real numbers; its sample space must be continuous, never discrete. Continuous random variables typically represent measured data — e.g. height, weight, or temperature. Continuous distributions are covered in a later topic; this topic focuses entirely on discrete random variables.
Random Variable→ PMF p(x) & CDF F(x)→ Expectation & Variance→ Named Discrete Distributions→ Bernoulli / Binomial / Multinomial / Poisson
The building blocks

Before naming any specific distribution, you need two general tools that describe any discrete random variable: the probability mass function, which gives the probability of each individual value, and the cumulative distribution function, which accumulates those probabilities.
Probability mass function (PMF)

Probability mass function, p(x) For a discrete random variable X, the PMF p(x) (also written f(x)) gives the probability that X takes exactly the value x, i.e. p(x) = P(X = x). Together with the possible values of X, the PMF constitutes the probability distribution of X.
Properties every valid PMF must satisfy
Non-negativity
p(x) ≥ 0 for every possible value x. A probability can never be negative.
Total probability
Σ p(x) = 1, summed over all possible values of x. The probabilities of every outcome the variable can take must add up to exactly 1.
To find the probability that X falls in a range, simply sum the PMF over that range: P(a ≤ X ≤ b) = Σa≤x≤b p(x).
Cumulative distribution function (CDF)

Cumulative distribution function, F(x) The CDF of a random variable X, denoted F(x), gives the probability that X takes a value less than or equal to x: F(x) = P(X ≤ x) For a discrete random variable with PMF p(x), the CDF is obtained by summing the PMF over all values t up to and including x: F(x) = Σt≤x p(t) Because it only changes at the discrete values X can take, the CDF of a discrete random variable is a step function.
Properties of the CDF

items: 1Non-decreasing: F(a) ≤ F(b) whenever a ≤ b — the CDF never goes down as x increases.
2Limits: as x → −∞, F(x) → 0; as x → ∞, F(x) → 1 — the CDF sweeps from "no probability accumulated" to "all probability accumulated."
3Bounded: 0 ≤ F(x) ≤ 1 for every x, since F(x) is itself a probability.

blocks.x: Building a CDF from a PMF
A discrete random variable X has the PMF: p(0) = 1/4, p(1) = 1/8, p(2) = 1/2, p(3) = 1/8. Find the CDF F(x) at each value of x.

items: 5F(3) = p(0) + p(1) + p(2) + p(3) — all probability accumulated.F(3) = 7/8 + 1/8 = 1

blocks.x: Answer: F(0)=1/4, F(1)=3/8, F(2)=7/8, F(3)=1 — note F climbs step by step and finishes at exactly 1, as required.
The discrete uniform distribution

Discrete uniform distribution The simplest discrete random variable: X assumes each of n values x₁, x₂, …, xₙ with equal probability, so p(xᵢ) = 1/n for i = 1, 2, …, n. When the values are the consecutive integers a, a+1, …, b (a ≤ b), the PMF is: P(X = k) = 1 / (b − a + 1), for k = a, a+1, …, b

Mean and variance of the discrete uniform For X uniform on {a, a+1, …, b}: E(X) = μ = (b + a) / 2 — simply the average of the first and last integers. Var(X) = σ² = [(b − a + 1)² − 1] / 12 — depends only on n = b − a + 1, the number of integers. Special case (standard discrete uniform, a = 1, b = n): E(X) = (n+1)/2, Var(X) = (n² − 1)/12.
Let X be uniform on {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}. Find E(X) and Var(X).

items: 1Identify a and b.a = 1, b = 5
2Apply the mean formula.E(X) = (5+1)/2 = 6/2 = 3
3Apply the variance formula.Var(X) = [(5−1+1)² − 1] / 12 = (25 − 1)/12 = 24/12 = 2

blocks.x: Answer: E(X) = 3, Var(X) = 2.

items: PMF p(x) answers "what is the probability of exactly this value?" — P(X = x).
CDF F(x) answers "what is the probability of this value or anything smaller?" — P(X ≤ x).
You can always recover P(X = x) from the CDF: for consecutive integer values, p(x) = F(x) − F(x−1).
The CDF of a discrete random variable is a staircase (step function): flat between possible values, then it jumps up by p(x) exactly at each value x can take.

sections.title: Expected value (mean) of a discrete random variable

blocks.x: Summarising a distribution in two numbers

A full PMF table can be unwieldy to work with. The expected value tells you the long-run average outcome, and the variance tells you how spread out the outcomes are around that average — together they summarise almost everything you need for decision-making.
Expected value (mean) of a discrete random variable

Expected value, E(X) The expected value (or mean, μ) of a discrete random variable X with PMF p(x) is the probability-weighted average of all its possible values: E(X) = μ = Σ x · p(x), summed over all possible values of x. It represents the long-run average value of X if the random experiment were repeated indefinitely.

Second moment, E(X²) The second moment about zero is found the same way, but with x² in place of x: E(X²) = Σ x² · p(x). It is not a probability itself — it is an intermediate quantity used to compute the variance.
Variance of a discrete random variable

Variance, Var(X) The variance (σ²) measures how spread out the values of X are around the mean: Var(X) = σ² = E(X²) − [E(X)]² A small variance means the outcomes cluster tightly around μ; a large variance means they are widely scattered. The standard deviation is σ = √Var(X), expressed in the same units as X.
Computing E(X), E(X²) and Var(X) from a PMF
Using the same PMF as before — p(0) = 1/4, p(1) = 1/8, p(2) = 1/2, p(3) = 1/8 — find E(X), E(X²) and Var(X).
Answer: E(X) = 1.5, E(X²) = 3.25, Var(X) = 1.
Reading E(X) and Var(X) in practice

In a quality-control or clinical setting, E(X) tells staff the expected number of an event (e.g. expected number of defective test kits in a batch, expected number of patient arrivals per hour), while Var(X) (or its square root, the standard deviation) tells them how much that number is likely to fluctuate from period to period — information that feeds directly into staffing, stock, and quality-assurance decisions.

blocks.title: Common pitfalls when computing E(X) and Var(X)

items: Forgetting to square x when computing E(X²) — it is Σx²p(x), not [Σx·p(x)]².
Confusing Var(X) with E(X²) — variance is E(X²) minus the square of the mean, not E(X²) alone.
Variance can never be negative; if your calculation gives a negative Var(X), check your arithmetic — you have made an error.
For named distributions (Bernoulli, Binomial, Poisson, etc.) you rarely need to sum a PMF by hand — each has ready-made mean/variance formulas, covered in the next two tabs.

blocks.x: Two outcomes, repeated

Many clinical and quality-control questions boil down to a yes/no outcome repeated many times: dead or alive after surgery, defective or not, male or female at birth. The Bernoulli distribution models a single such trial; the Binomial distribution models counting the successes across many independent repeats.
The Bernoulli process

Bernoulli trial & Bernoulli process A single trial of an experiment that can result in one of two mutually exclusive outcomes — e.g. head or tail, yes or no, dead or alive, male or female — is called a Bernoulli trial. A sequence of such trials forms a Bernoulli process.
Every Bernoulli process must satisfy

items: 1Each trial results in one of two mutually exclusive outcomes: success or failure.
2The probability of success, p, remains constant from trial to trial. The probability of failure is q = 1 − p.
3The trials are independent — the outcome of one trial does not affect any other.
4The random variable of the experiment is binary, taking only the values 0 and 1.

blocks.x: The Bernoulli distribution

Bernoulli distribution A random variable X has a Bernoulli distribution if it takes the value 1 for "success" (probability p) and 0 for "failure" (probability q = 1 − p): p(x) = p if x = 1, and p(x) = q = 1 − p if x = 0 Equivalently, in one compact formula: p(x) = pˣ(1 − p)¹⁻ˣ, for x = 0, 1.

Mean, variance & MGF of the Bernoulli distribution Mean: E(X) = μ = p Variance: Var(X) = σ² = p(1 − p) Moment generating function: MX(t) = pet + q (Derived from E(X) = 0·q + 1·p = p, and E(X²) = 0²·q + 1²·p = p, so Var(X) = E(X²) − [E(X)]² = p − p² = p(1−p).)
The Binomial distribution

Binomial distribution The Binomial distribution models experiments consisting of identical, independent Bernoulli trials, and is used to count the number of successes across n trials — e.g. tossing a coin n times and counting heads, or testing n items and counting defectives.
Every Binomial experiment must satisfy

items: 1The experiment consists of n independent and identical trials.
2Each trial results in one of two outcomes: success or failure.
3The probability of success, p, is the same in every trial; probability of failure is q = 1 − p.
4The random variable of interest, X, is the number of successes observed across the n trials.

blocks.x: Binomial PMF A random variable X has a Binomial distribution based on n trials with probability of success p if: P(X = x) = C(n, x) pˣ (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ, for x = 0, 1, 2, …, n, where 0 < p < 1. Here C(n, x) = n! / [x!(n−x)!] is the number of ways to choose which x of the n trials are "successes." Notation: X ~ B(n, p).
Mean and variance of the Binomial distribution μ = E(X) = np σ² = Var(X) = np(1 − p)
Political preference survey

25% of the inhabitants of a community favour political party A. A random sample of 20 inhabitants is selected, and each is asked whether they will vote for party A. Find (i) P(exactly 2 vote for A), (ii) P(at least 3 vote for A), (iii) P(fewer than 2 vote for A).

items: 1Identify the model and parameters.X = number who favour A, X ~ B(n = 20, p = 0.25), q = 0.75

blocks.x: Quality control of hospital test kits

A hospital receives disposable test kits with a manufacturer-stated defective rate of 3%. A laboratory inspector randomly selects 20 kits for inspection. Find (i) P(exactly 3 are defective), (ii) P(not more than 2 are defective).

items: 1Identify the model. Let Y = number of defective kits.Y ~ B(n = 20, p = 0.03)

blocks.x: Answer: (i) ≈ 0.0183, (ii) ≈ 0.9790. Note the mean number of defective kits is E(Y) = np = 20 × 0.03 = 0.6 — most inspection batches will have 0 or 1 defective kit.

items: Bernoulli: a single trial, X ∈ {0, 1}, mean = p, variance = p(1−p).
Binomial: n independent, identical Bernoulli trials, X = number of successes ∈ {0, 1, …, n}, mean = np, variance = np(1−p).
A Bernoulli distribution is exactly the special case of the Binomial with n = 1.
Both require a constant success probability p and independent trials — if p changes trial to trial, or trials are not independent, neither model applies.

blocks.x: Beyond two outcomes, and counting rare events

Not every trial is a simple yes/no, and not every count comes from a fixed number of trials. The Multinomial distribution generalises the Binomial to more than two outcomes per trial, while the Poisson distribution counts how many times a rare, random event occurs in a fixed interval of time, space or volume.
The Multinomial experiment

Multinomial distribution The Multinomial distribution is the generalisation of the Binomial to trials with more than two possible outcomes (k > 2), where the probability of each outcome is the same on every trial. Examples: an opinion poll where respondents are "for," "against," or "undecided"; a product rated "excellent," "very good," "good," "average," or "inferior."
Conditions of a Multinomial experiment

items: 1The experiment consists of n independent, identical trials.
2Each trial results in one of k mutually exclusive outcomes, with probabilities p₁, p₂, …, pₖ such that Σpⱼ = 1.
3The probability pᵢ of each outcome i remains constant across all trials.

blocks.x: Multinomial random variables & joint PMF Let y₁, y₂, …, yₖ denote the number of trials falling into each of the k categories, with y₁ + y₂ + … + yₖ = n. The joint probability of observing exactly this combination is: P(y₁, y₂, …, yₖ) = n! / (y₁! y₂! ⋯ yₖ!) · p₁y₁ p₂y₂ ⋯ pₖyₖ where each yⱼ = 0, 1, …, n, Σyⱼ = n, and Σpⱼ = 1.

Moments of the Multinomial distribution E(yⱼ) = npⱼ Var(yⱼ) = npⱼ(1 − pⱼ) Cov(yᵢ, yⱼ) = −npᵢpⱼ (for i ≠ j) The negative covariance reflects that categories compete for the same n trials — more outcomes falling into one category necessarily means fewer falling into the others.
Quality control in a hospital laboratory

A batch of diagnostic test kits: 70% are defect-free, 20% have a Type A defect (minor calibration error), and 10% have a Type B defect (major functional error). Six kits are randomly selected. Find the probability that exactly 3 are defect-free, 1 has a Type A defect, and 2 have a Type B defect.

items: 1Set up the model: multinomial with n = 6, k = 3 categories.y₁ = 3, y₂ = 1, y₃ = 2; p₁ = 0.70, p₂ = 0.20, p₃ = 0.10
2Apply the multinomial PMF.P(y₁,y₂,y₃) = 6!/(3!1!2!) × (0.70)³ (0.20)¹ (0.10)²
3Evaluate the multinomial coefficient and powers.6!/(3!1!2!) = 60; (0.70)³ = 0.343; (0.20)¹ = 0.20; (0.10)² = 0.01
4Multiply everything together.P = 60 × 0.343 × 0.20 × 0.01 = 0.04116

blocks.x: Answer: P ≈ 0.04116 — about a 4.12% chance of observing exactly this combination.
The Poisson distribution

Poisson process The Poisson distribution models a discrete random variable counting the number of times a particular event occurs during a fixed unit of time, area, or volume — the underlying random mechanism is called a Poisson process.
Conditions of a Poisson process

items: 1Randomness and independence: the occurrence (or non-occurrence) of the event in any interval of time, space, or volume is random and independent of its occurrence in any other, non-overlapping interval.
2Rare events: an unlimited number of occurrences is theoretically possible in the interval, but in any infinitesimally small sub-interval, the probability of more than one occurrence is negligible.
3Proportionality: the probability of the event occurring in a given interval is proportional to the length of that interval.
4Mean = variance: the mean number of events in an interval, μ, is equal to its variance.

blocks.x: Typical Poisson experiments
Clinical / operational
Number of patients arriving at an emergency department in a given period; number of industrial accidents in a period; number of insurance claims received in a period.
Other classic examples

Number of radioactive particles emitted in a period; number of errors in typing a page of text; number of repairs needed on a kilometre of road; number of telephone calls received in a unit time interval.
In every example, the random variable represents the number of events occurring in a unit period of time or space, during which the mean number of events, μ, is expected to occur.

Poisson PMF The Poisson distribution for the random variable X, representing the number of occurrences of an event in a given interval, is: P(X = x) = μˣ e⁻ᵘ / x!, for x = 0, 1, 2, …, and μ > 0. Mean and variance are equal: E(X) = μ = Var(X). Notation: X ~ P(μ).
Patient arrivals at an emergency desk

Patients arrive at an emergency desk at an average rate of 4 per minute, following a Poisson process. Find (i) P(no patient arrives in one minute), (ii) P(at least 2 patients arrive in one minute), (iii) P(at least 3 patients arrive in two minutes).

items: 1Identify the model. X ~ Poisson(λ), λ = mean number of arrivals per interval.For one minute: λ = 4
4(iii) Rescale λ for a two-minute interval: λ = 4 × 2 = 8.P(X≥3) = 1 − [P(0)+P(1)+P(2)] = 1 − [e⁻⁸ + 8e⁻⁸ + 32e⁻⁸] = 1 − 41e⁻⁸

blocks.x: Poisson approximation to the Binomial distribution

Why approximate? When the number of trials n in a Binomial process is large, computing exact binomial probabilities (with large factorials and tiny powers) becomes tedious. The Poisson distribution provides a good, much simpler approximation. This approximation is valid when n is large and p is small — the classic setting for rare events observed over many trials.

The approximation theorem Let X ~ B(n, p). If n → ∞ and p → 0 in such a way that np = μ stays fixed and positive, then: C(n, x) pˣ (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ˣ ≈ μˣ e⁻ᵘ / x!, where p = μ/n In practice: set μ = np and use the Poisson PMF in place of the Binomial PMF.
Rare adverse events in a large population

The probability that a patient develops a complication after exposure to a risk factor is 0.00015. Of 20,000 exposed patients, find (i) the expected number who develop the complication, (ii) the probability that at least one patient develops the complication.

items: 1Identify parameters. This is Binomial with n = 20,000, p = 0.00015 — n is huge and p tiny, so use the Poisson approximation.n = 20,000, p = 0.00015
2(i) E(X) = np sets μ for the Poisson approximation.E(X) = np = 20,000 × 0.00015 = 3, so λ = μ = 3
3(ii) P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − P(X = 0), using the Poisson PMF.P(X ≥ 1) = 1 − e⁻³ ≈ 1 − 0.0498 = 0.9502

blocks.x: Answer: (i) E(X) = 3 expected complications, (ii) P(X ≥ 1) ≈ 0.9502 (95.0%).

blocks.title: Choosing the right distribution — quick decision guide

items: Bernoulli: a single yes/no trial.
Binomial: a fixed number of independent yes/no trials (n known, p constant); X = number of successes.
Multinomial: a fixed number of independent trials, but each trial has more than two possible outcomes.
Poisson: counting events over a fixed interval of time/space/volume, with no fixed number of trials — events occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate μ.

Poisson approximating Binomial: you technically have a Binomial(n, p), but n is very large and p is very small (np = μ moderate) — use the Poisson formula with λ = np instead of computing the exact Binomial probability.
